transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-25 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~57 minutes
Attendees: Ava Patel (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Lisa Chen (CrestPay Head of ML), Mark Rivera (Platform), Samir Gupta (CTO)

[00:00] Ava: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick intros, we can jump into the Optimize walkthrough — batching, prefix/KV caching, and the cost model we ran for CrestPay. Diego will drive the technical parts.
[00:12] Lisa: Thanks, Ava. We appreciate this; main things for us are P95 latency under 120ms for UI auth flows, and trying to keep unit cost so we can scale to 10M monthly requests.
[00:22] Diego: Great, noted. Mark, Samir, feel free to jump in — we'll call out assumptions in the cost examples but want to hear about your traffic patterns.
[00:30] Mark: Most flows are short context: payment confirmation, fraud check prompts, usually 120-300 tokens each. We do some long context stuff for dispute histories but it's <5% of traffic.
[00:40] Samir: And infra-wise, we're running on k8s in AWS (EKS), mostly g4dn for model endpoints today, but open to dedicated GPU pools if it improves predictability. Data residency is US only.
[00:52] Diego: Perfect. First slide — quick refresher on batching: continuous batching at the runtime level increases GPU utilization, reduces per-token cost but adds queueing latency. We tune two knobs: max_batch_size and max_queue_time.
[01:10] Diego: Example: if you set max_queue_time to 10ms and max_batch_size 32, you get good throughput with sub-100ms added tail in many cases. If you push max_queue_time to 50ms you get more throughput but your P95 shifts.
[01:27] Lisa: Can Redwood do adaptive policies? We can't have a static knob that kills the UI.
[01:32] Diego: Yep — we have workload-aware policies. For interactive UI flows we bias towards low queue time and lower batch sizes, for async backfills we prefer larger batches.
[01:40] Ava: Ok, next: prefix caching and KV cache. Two separate patterns. Prefix caching is for repeated prefixes — e.g., system prompts, templates for payment confirmation — where you cache the KV state for the prefix across requests. KV cache is more explicit: store embeddings or intermediate KV states keyed by conversation id or user id.
[01:56] Mark: For us, payment confirmations share a long system prompt plus a few user slots that change. Sounds like prefix caching is a good fit.
[02:04] Diego: Exactly. In our cost model we assumed a 70% prefix hit rate for those flows which, combined with moderate batching, yielded about 3x token-cost reduction compared to no cache.
[02:14] Samir: That 70% number — optimistic. How sensitive are the savings to hit rate?
[02:18] Diego: Very sensitive. At 50% you still get ~2x savings; at 30% the benefits drop but still non-trivial. The cost model spreadsheet I'll share breaks this down. Main drivers: average prefix length, cache key cardinality, and eviction TTL.
[02:31] Lisa: What's eviction TTL typical? We have many unique sessions but repeated templates across accounts.
[02:36] Diego: For templates, TTL can be high — minutes to hours. For per-session KV entries we use shorter TTL, maybe 5-15 minutes, because they blow up cardinality.
[02:44] Ava: To ground this, we made a small worked example in the spreadsheet: CrestPay example traffic — 70% short confirmation prompts at 150 tokens, 25% medium fraud-check at ~400 tokens, 5% long context. We compared: no cache + small batch vs prefix cache with same batch config vs prefix + KV mix.
[03:03] Diego: Slide math: baseline per-token cost of the model (open model on gpus) assumed X¢ per 1k tokens (we used an anonymized price to mirror your Orleans-run numbers), then applied throughput improvements. With prefix caching our per-request token generation dropped by ~60% for the short flows so tokens-per-request go from 150 to ~60 effective.
[03:24] Mark: Are you including added memory for KV caches on the GPU? We're limited on GPU memory on g4 instances.
[03:31] Diego: Good call — yes the cost model includes memory overhead and slight throughput penalty for KV cache lookups. For very memory constrained setups we recommend prefix caching first (smaller memory footprint) and then evaluate tiny per-shard KV caches.
[03:44] Lisa: How does this differ if we go Redwood Dedicated? We want predictable throughput and SLA.
[03:49] Ava: Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools so throughput and latency are predictable. The cost model shows similar % savings from caching, but total cost moves from usage-based to a blend of reserved commit plus less variable token cost. For scale, Dedicated typically lowers unit costs at steady state.
[04:05] Diego: Also, Dedicated lets you pin model variants and quantization (4-bit) which reduces GPU memory and improves throughput; that affects both batching and caching economics.
[04:15] Samir: We asked security — SOC2, SSO, KMS — are those handled for Dedicated?
[04:20] Ava: Yes: Dedicated + Private deployments support customer-managed KMS, VPC peering, and the audit logs you need. We'll send the security pack.
[04:27] Lisa: Back to tuning — you mentioned dynamic batching policies. Is that automatic or do we need to instrument with custom metrics?
[04:33] Diego: Redwood runtime auto-batches, but the routing and policy layer uses telemetry to adjust. We suggest starting with our recommended profile: interactive profile (queue_time 10ms, batch_size 16) for UI, background profile (queue_time 40ms, batch_size 64) for async. We'll share the config.
[04:49] Mark: For our fraud-check flows where we need slightly longer context, would prefix caching still help?
[04:55] Diego: Yes, if there's a stable prefix (system prompt + product details). For long conversation histories you might combine prefix caching for the repeated system part and KV cache for session-level tokens.
[05:05] Ava: Let's walk through the numbers we prepared for CrestPay — Diego, can you summarize the cost model slide?
[05:09] Diego: Sure — baseline scenario: 1M short confirmation requests/day, avg 150 tokens request+resp. Baseline token cost (anonymized) = $Y per 1M tokens. With prefix cache hit rate 70% and batching tuned to interactive profile we estimate effective token consumption drops to ~40-60% of baseline, netting ~2.5-3x savings. If you add Dedicated + 4-bit quantization we push that further since throughput capacity improves and we reduce per-token infer cost.
[05:36] Lisa: Any caveats on quality when quantizing? We can't regress on accuracy for fraud-checks.
[05:40] Diego: Always test — in our experience 4-bit performs well for many open models, but we'd run a small eval set (we can run it for you) to measure any regressions and only recommend quantization if regression <1-2% on your eval metrics.
[05:53] Samir: Can we run a POC with our real traffic?
[05:56] Ava: Yes — typical POC: we mirror traffic for 24-72 hours into a dedicated pool and run with and without prefix caching to capture real hit rates and cost/latency. Diego will size the pool.
[06:07] Mark: What instrumentation do you need from us?
[06:10] Diego: Ideally: sample prompts, token distribution, and a sketch of session ids or conversation grouping rules. If you can't share production data we can synthesize based on distributions.
[06:20] Lisa: We'll share sample prompts and traffic break down; privacy notes — we'll scrub PII first.
[06:24] Ava: Great. Quick Q&A — competitors and licensing?
[06:28] Samir: We tried some OpenAI streaming and it was easy, but cost got high. How is Redwood different?
[06:33] Ava: Redwood is inference-first — we focus on serving economics and predictable latency across hosted/dedicated/private. Our Optimize tooling recommends batching and caching settings automatically and ties them to cost models so you can decide tradeoffs.
[06:45] Mark: Any gotchas with EKS and peering?
[06:48] Diego: For Private deployment we do VPC peering and provide an agent; main network considerations are egress for metrics and access to customer KMS if using CMEK.
[06:58] Lisa: Can you share examples of prefix cache config?
[07:01] Diego: Yes — we'll include a sample: identify stable prefix tokens (system prompts + template sections), configure prefix TTL, and set a cache key strategy (e.g., template_id + region). We'll annotate the spreadsheet with suggested TTLs and expected hit rates.
[07:13] Ava: Ok let's recap actions and timelines. Diego will prepare the Dedicated sizing and POC plan; I'll send the spreadsheet and sample configs; CrestPay will provide prompts & traffic distribution. Then we'll schedule the POC for early April.
[07:24] Lisa: Sounds good. Any final questions?
[07:28] Samir: One last: does Redwood support automatic fallback to smaller model if pool is saturated?
[07:33] Diego: Yes — routing policies can fallback to cheaper model variants with degraded but acceptable quality. We can configure per-route fallbacks.
[07:39] Ava: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the deck, spreadsheet and security docs.
[07:44] Mark: Appreciate it.
[07:46] Lisa: Thanks, bye.

End transcript.
Notes: transcription has minor inaccuracies (speaker overlaps, some model names anonymized). References to pricing anonymized per CrestPay NDA.
